# Expansion: Vannevar Bush and Research Policy
The narrative of scientific leadership highlights **Vannevar Bush** (1890–1974), a pivotal figure who bridged engineering innovation with national research policy. An MIT professor and inventor known for the **differential analyzer** , Bush initially focused on "hard science" at the Carnegie Institution, ethically removing the Eugenics Record Office to prioritize technical research. His influence expanded to federal policy and wartime efforts; as a member of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA), he advocated for the Ames Research Center. Responding to World War I coordination failures, he founded the **National Defense Research Committee (NDRC)** in 1940, streamlining operations, fostering British collaboration, and overseeing radar and the Radiation Laboratory.
When Roosevelt established the **Office of Scientific Research and Development (OSRD)** in 1941, Bush became its director. Managing hundreds of millions in contracts and coordinating diverse agencies, he ensured civilian scientists remained distinct from the military. His leadership was instrumental in the **Manhattan Project** , where he persuaded Roosevelt to fund and oversee the atomic bomb program, manage UK cooperation, and later advise on its use against Japan. He witnessed the Trinity test and promoted post-war scientific openness to prevent nuclear arms races. Notably, Bush is also renowned for his 1945 essay *"As We May Think,"* which introduced the **memex** —a microfilm-based, associative memory device widely considered a precursor to the World Wide Web. This visionary essay later influenced the development of the mouse, hypertext, and modern information science.
Following World War II, Bush advocated for a strong government role in basic research, leading to the creation of the **National Science Foundation (NSF)** in 1950, though his preferred independent agency was pocket-vetoed. He served as chairman of the Joint Research and Development Board and later the Research and Development Board, significantly shaping defense research policies and international arms control discussions. Despite his influential legacy, his authority declined as he navigated corporate boards, university trusteeships, and government panels. He died in 1974, recognized by Jerome Wiesner as having the greatest influence on the growth of science and technology in the United States.
Bush's contributions were recognized with numerous accolades, including the Edison Medal (1943), National Medal of Science (1963), and the Atomic Pioneers Award (1970). His enduring impact is memorialized through the Vannevar Bush Award, established by the NSF in 1980, and the preservation of his papers at institutions like the Library of Congress. Additionally, his life and work have been portrayed by actors Jonathan Hale and Matthew Modine in films.
